newsitem.title: CANADA: BANK OF CANADA SEES LESS NEED FOR MONETARY EASING.
newsitem.headline: BANK OF CANADA SEES LESS NEED FOR MONETARY EASING.

text.p: The slack in the Canadian economy is shrinking, meaning Canada's central bank will have less need to promote easy monetary conditions, the Bank of Canada said in its Summer Review released Tuesday.
"As economic slack is taken up, the Bank will need to promote less accommodative monetary conditions in order to preserve a durable, non-inflationary expansion," the Review said.
The bank said it expects inflation to stick to the lower half of the bank's target range of one to three percent for the rest of 1997.
Inflation was pegged at 2.0 percent for the month of May.
The bank said dthat even though the excess capacity in the Canadian economy is shrinking, there will still be an "appreciable margin of slack" in 1997 and 1998.
The report estimated that the output gap -- or the excess capacity in the Canadian economy -- stands at about 2-1/4 percent at the end of the first quarter.
The closer an economy gets to full capacity, or eliminating the output gap, the higher the likelihood of inflationary pressures.
The Bank of Canada raised its key interest rate by 25 basis points on June 26, the bank's first rate hike in more than a year. The hike was mainly in response to a weakening Canadian dollar.
The rate hike gave a boost to the currency, but it has since weakened again.
But the bank said on Tuesday it expects a stronger Canadian dollar in the future.
"Canada's strong underlying economic fundamentals continue to support market expectations that the Canadian dollar will appreciate over time," the report said.
The bank forecasted strong growth in domestic demand, production and job creation, especiallly in the private sector.
The report also predicted a moderage upward trend in commodity prices in the coming months, supporting Canadian production and exports.
"External and domestic factors point to continued robust expansion and further employment gains in coming months," the report said.
Overall, the bank predicted an average rate of economic expansion of four percent through to the fourth quarter of 1997.
The bank was also optimistic about Canadian financial markets despite the recent volatility of the currency.
"Despoite recent fluctuations of the exchange rate, Canadian financial markets continute to be supported by the positive fundamentals underlying the Canadian economy," the report said.

In previous reports, the Bank of Canada said it needed to keep a close watch on M1 -- the narrowest measure of money supply in the Canadian economy -- because it was growing rapidly, which could lead to future inflationary pressure.
The bank said in its summer review that M1 must still be watched closely in the months ahead.

"The recent acceleration in M1 growth would be in line with a return of the Canadian economy to full capacity," the report said. "However, if such strong growth were to persist into 1998, it would not be consistent with maintaining low inflation."
Broader measures of the money supply show a rate of growth consistent with keeping low inflation in the bottom half of the bank's target range, the report said.
Most of Canada's major trading partners were expected to expand modestly with low inflation, the bank said.
The report said it could not rule out a further tightening of U.S. monetary conditions before the end of the year.
((Heather Scoffield, Reuters Ottawa Bureau 613 235-6745))
